questions.q: What is the main finding of the research described?
options: Most people respond to medications identically, so genetic testing adds little to prescribing
Only people of European ancestry carry gene variants that change drug response, so testing is limited
Nearly everyone carries gene variants that can affect drug response, so testing may improve prescribing
Gene variants affect drug response in about 1 in 100 people, so testing is rarely worthwhile
questions.explain: The team found virtually all participants carried relevant variants, suggesting broader testing may help optimize medications.

questions.q: Why do researchers know less about key gene variants in many groups?
options: Those groups have mostly declined to enroll in large genetic studies
Most genetic research has involved people of European ancestry
Their genomes are harder to sequence with standard research equipment
Health records for those groups are rarely kept in research databases
questions.explain: The passage says most genetic research was done on people of European ancestry.

questions.q: About what share of participants had taken a drug affected by a genetic variant they carried?
questions.explain: About 24% had taken a drug affected by a variant they carried.

questions.q: How many previously unreported variants did the team identify?
questions.explain: The team identified 17,704 previously unreported variants in protein-coding regions of the genes.

questions.q: Why does the author say the 24% figure likely underestimates the true rate?
options: Participants hid some of their medications
Only 16 genes were examined by the models
questions.explain: The passage says because health records can be incomplete, the results likely underestimate actual gene-drug interactions.
